title: Jeremiah 25:1–14
context: The narrator dates this word to Jehoiakim’s fourth year, which it equates with Nebuchadnezzar’s first year, and Jeremiah then speaks to all Judah and Jerusalem, reviewing twenty-three years of preaching that went unheard, before he reports the LORD’s word: Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant,” will come against the land, joy will be silenced, and “these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.” The LORD also promises to punish Babylon in turn when the seventy years are accomplished (cf. 29:10; 2 Chr 36:21; Dan 9:2), and how the seventy years are reckoned is discussed rather than settled. Both traditions share the ground that the LORD rules over the nations, judges persistent unbelief, and also holds Babylon accountable, and the question of how God uses an evil agent points to the existing box at Judges 9:23 rather than a new one.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (this was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),
verses.arminianNotes:
The word came “in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (this was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon).” Arminian readers note that the narrator ties Judah’s history to Babylon’s rise.

The same year is named in 36:1 and 46:2; exact dating is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophetic word anchored in real history.

Shared ground: both traditions read the date as setting this sermon at a turning point, when Babylon’s power was rising, while hedging precise calendar conversions.

verses.text: which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah, and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem:
verses.arminianNotes:
The word is one “which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah, and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the word is addressed to the whole people.

Jeremiah speaks publicly, not only to the king or the leaders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet sent to the whole covenant community.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the word is public and that the people as a whole are responsible to hear it, with Jeremiah named as the one who speaks.

verses.text: From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, even to this day, these twenty-three years, the LORD’s word has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising up early and speaking; but you have not listened.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says, “From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, even to this day, these twenty-three years, the LORD’s word has come to me.” Arminian readers note the long patience of the LORD (cf. 1:2).

The people had many opportunities to listen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s long-suffering in sending his word year after year.

Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase “rising up early and speaking” as an image of earnest, persistent warning, and both note the sober verdict, “but you have not listened.”

verses.text: The LORD has sent to you all his servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them (but you have not listened or inclined your ear to hear),
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD has sent to you all his servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them.” Arminian readers note that Jeremiah stands in a long line of prophets whose call to return was real.

The refusal is the people’s own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise affirm the sincerity of the prophetic call and the people’s responsibility for refusing it.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s word came faithfully and that Judah’s failure to listen is not God’s fault.

verses.text: saying, “Return now everyone from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings, and dwell in the land that the LORD has given to you and to your fathers, from of old and even forever more.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophets said, “Return now everyone from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings, and dwell in the land.” Arminian readers note that the call to return comes with a promise of continued life in the land.

They read it as a genuine offer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a real call to repentance joined to covenant promise.

Shared ground: both traditions read the summons to return as earnest and gracious, and both note that the land is described as given “from of old and even forever more.”

verses.text: Don’t go after other gods to serve them or worship them, and don’t provoke me to anger with the work of your hands; then I will do you no harm.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t go after other gods to serve them or worship them, and don’t provoke me to anger with the work of your hands; then I will do you no harm.” Arminian readers note the conditional promise.

Idolatry is named as the central offense.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the first commandment at the heart of the call.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that idolatry provokes the LORD and that obedience would have brought protection rather than harm.

verses.text: “Yet you have not listened to me,” says the LORD, “that you may provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own hurt.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet you have not listened to me,” says the LORD. Arminian readers note that the people’s idolatry is described as working “to your own hurt.”

Their refusal harms them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see sin bringing its own damage on the sinner.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s warnings were for the people’s good, and that their refusal, not God’s unwillingness, brought the coming harm.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD of Armies says: “Because you have not heard my words,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says, “Because you have not heard my words.” Arminian readers note that judgment follows from refusal to hear.

The “therefore” links the sentence to the long history just described.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment as the just response to persistent unbelief.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a turning from warning to sentence, grounded in the people’s refusal over many years.

verses.text: behold, I will send and take all the families of the north,” says the LORD, “and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all these nations around. I will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and a hissing, and perpetual desolations.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I will send to Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” (cf. 27:6; 43:10). Arminian readers note that the title marks his role as an instrument of judgment, not approval of his character.

God directs evil already chosen by human agents.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the king as serving God’s purpose, and they hold that God ordains and governs such events without being the author of sin.

Shared ground: both traditions agree Babylon remains accountable (25:12).

verses.text: Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.” Arminian readers note the silencing of ordinary joy (cf. 7:34).

The millstones and lamp picture daily life ceasing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the grief of judgment touching homes and households.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with sorrow, noting that judgment is not abstract but reaches weddings, work, and the evening lamp.

verses.text: This whole land will be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that “these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years.” Arminian readers note that the seventy years appear again in 29:10, 2 Chr 36:21, and Dan 9:2.

Some count from Babylon’s early dominance, others from the temple’s fall; many read a round figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the reckoning lightly and do not harmonize the passages into one scheme.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the number shows the judgment is limited and under God’s control, and that the exact counting is discussed.

verses.text: “It will happen, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation,” says the LORD, “for their iniquity. I will make the land of the Chaldeans desolate forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
“It will happen, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation,” says the LORD. Arminian readers note that the instrument of judgment is itself judged.

Babylon is held responsible for its iniquity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s justice reaching the very power he used.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that being used by God does not excuse Babylon’s evil.

verses.text: I will bring on that land all my words which I have pronounced against it, even all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah has prophesied against all the nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will bring on Babylon “all my words which I have pronounced against it, even all that is written in this book.” Arminian readers note the reference to a written collection of oracles.

Some Greek traditions place the oracles against the nations after this verse and in a different order; this site follows the English order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that difference as an observation and do not build a doctrine on either order.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming that the LORD’s written word against the nations will come to pass.

verses.text: For many nations and great kings will make bondservants of them, even of them. I will recompense them according to their deeds, and according to the work of their hands.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For many nations and great kings will make bondservants of them, even of them.” Arminian readers note the reversal: Babylon, which enslaved others, will be enslaved.

The LORD says, “I will recompense them according to their deeds.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s just recompense on Babylon’s deeds.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God judges according to works and that no empire stands beyond his reach.
